title: He was doing everything right… and still ended up in chains.
paragraphs: He was doing everything right… and still ended up in chains.
Let that bother you for a second.

Because deep down, we’ve believed a quiet lie:
If God is with me, life should be working.

Open doors.
Clear answers.
Visible progress.

But what do you do when obedience leads you… not to promotion—
but to a prison?

Joseph didn’t flirt with sin—he ran from it.
He honored his master. He feared God. He chose righteousness when no one was watching.

And still—
he was falsely accused.
Stripped of dignity.
Thrown into a dark cell.

No applause.
No explanation.
No timeline.
Just silence.
Here’s the part we don’t like to say out loud:
Sometimes your worst season comes right after your greatest obedience.
Sit with that.

Because if your theology only works when life is smooth—
it won’t survive the prison.
But Scripture refuses to let us misinterpret Joseph’s story.
“But the Lord was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love…” — Genesis 39:21

Not after the prison.
Not once things improved.
In it.
God didn’t step out when Joseph stepped in.
So why do we?

Why do we assume that when life gets heavy—
God got distant?

Why do we interpret delay as denial…
silence as absence…
pain as punishment?
Let me speak straight to your spirit:
Your struggle is not evidence that God left you.

It might be evidence that God is forming something in you
that comfort could never produce.
Because prisons in the Kingdom are never pointless.

They are hidden classrooms.
Sacred workshops.
Places where God does His deepest work—
when nobody is watching.

Joseph wasn’t just waiting in prison.
He was becoming.

Becoming resilient.
Becoming wise.
Becoming trustworthy with pressure.

Because where God was taking him—
palace-level purpose, nation-saving authority—
required prison-level formation.

Some scholars interpret this season as divine preparation—
that before God elevates a man publicly,
He shapes him privately.

Because elevation without formation
is destruction waiting to happen.
Let that hit:

Maybe the delay isn’t denial.
Maybe it’s mercy.

You’re asking,
“God, why am I here?”

And heaven is whispering,
“Because I love you too much to send you unprepared.”
But let’s go deeper.

Because Joseph’s story is powerful—
but it’s not the center.
It points to Someone greater.
Jesus Christ

He was also innocent.
Also betrayed.
Also falsely accused.
But His “prison” wasn’t made of stone.

It was made of nails.
Wood.
And the full weight of human sin.
The cross looked like the ultimate contradiction.

The Son of God—
bleeding.
Mocked.
Crushed.
Where was God then?
Isaiah 53 tells us the truth:
“It was the will of the Lord to crush Him…”
Not abandonment.
Purpose.
Not failure.
Redemption.
Jesus didn’t just enter suffering.
He absorbed it.

He took your sin.
Your shame.
Your hidden failures.
Your silent guilt.
And He carried it to a place that looked like the end.
But it wasn’t the end.

Three days later—
the stone moved.
And in that moment, God declared something that still echoes today:
I am present, even in places that look like death.
So hear me clearly:

If you are in a hard season right now—
you are not forgotten.

If you feel stuck—
you are not forsaken.

If heaven feels quiet—
God is not absent.

He is with you in the tension.
With you in the waiting.
With you in the unanswered questions.

Working in ways you cannot yet see.
Building strength you will soon need.
Preparing doors you cannot yet access.
But here’s the invitation—don’t miss this.

Joseph trusted God in the prison.
Jesus surrendered to the Father at the cross.
Now it’s your turn.
Come back to Him.

Not when everything makes sense.
Not when the breakthrough arrives.
Now.

Repent of the areas you’ve drifted.
Release the need to control everything.
Trust Him in the middle—not just the miracle.

Because the same God who was with Joseph in the prison…
The same Savior who walked out of the grave…
is with you.

Right there.
Right now.

And one day—
you will look back at this season
that felt like it was breaking you…
and realize—
it was building you.
Be the reminder they didn’t know they needed.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
